entries.root_cause: The G1 successor-authorization manifest described a proposed authorization and a post-merge effect in prose-like fields but did not encode the repository-standard machine-readable implementation_authority_before_merge and implementation_authority_after_merge transition. Automated consumers could therefore not distinguish merge permission from the implementation authority that becomes effective only after canonicalization.

The first G1 authorization validator did not attest the manifest effective_rule, allowing a manifest-only mutation to claim immediate effect while all other exact-head authorization fields remained green. A merge-gated proposal therefore lacked a permanent executable assertion for its activation rule.

The initial G1 exact-scope validator checked only a subset of explicitly_not_authorized entries. Removing an unlisted exclusion such as browser long-lived credentials, ITSM, or production C3 numerics could therefore silently widen the successor authorization while the dedicated validator stayed green.

The G1 task packet delegated repository path selection to the later implementation PR, so post-merge implementation authority had a bounded capability but no pre-reviewed machine-readable file boundary. That allowed a future implementation to self-classify shared runtime, authority, contract, or governance paths as G1-specific without successor authorization.

The base learning resolver credited newly registered G1 falsifiers from entrypoint reachability alone. Without registering G1's must_fail helper in the strict falsifier-effects layer, a credited G1 function could be reduced to a no-op body while retaining its name and main-call shape, leaving the ledger apparently guarded.

The authorization manifest declared that future implementation diffs must obey the G1 path policy, but no canonical-base/exact-head workflow actually consumed that policy against a future implementation PR's complete diff. A mixed G1/shared-core PR could therefore violate the reviewed boundary without an executable gate.

The strict falsifier-effects registry verified that credited G1 falsifiers called a helper named must_fail, but did not execute that helper against both rejected and accepted mutations. The helper body itself could therefore be replaced by a no-op while every name/reachability check remained green.

The first future-G1 scope workflow executed the evaluator from the candidate PR HEAD. A candidate could therefore replace the workflow or validator that judged its own diff, converting the enforcement boundary into self-attestation.

The first G1 relevance rule inferred implementation intent only from a voluntary branch prefix or allowed G1 path. A candidate using an unrecognized branch and only shared-core changes could avoid classification, so omission of identifying metadata did not fail closed.

The executable implementation-diff finding was reconciled to a manifest-policy falsifier rather than a probe that exercised the actual Git diff gate. The real scope falsifier therefore could weaken while the ledger still reported the finding as guarded.
